Before diving in, let's quickly clarify what a phrasal verb is. A phrasal verb is a verb combined with one or more small words (like off, up, out, in) that together create a new meaning — a meaning that is often completely different from the original verb. For example, "put" means to place something somewhere, but "put off" means something entirely different. This is what makes phrasal verbs tricky, and why you need to learn them as whole units.
"Put Off" — The Core Idea

There is one simple image that connects almost all meanings of "put off": the idea of something being pushed away — either in time, or in feeling. Keep this image in mind, and the meanings will make much more sense.
Meaning 1: To Postpone (Delay Something to a Later Time)

This is the most common meaning.

When you put something off, you decide not to do it now and move it to a later time. You are essentially "pushing it away" into the future.

Examples:

  • "I have a dentist appointment tomorrow, but I'm going to put it off until next month." (I'll reschedule it for later.)
  • "She keeps putting off her homework and then panics at night."
  • "Don't put off important decisions — they don't disappear on their own."
  • "The match was put off because of heavy rain." (It was postponed.)

In everyday life, this meaning shows up constantly. Whenever people delay doing something unpleasant or difficult, they are "putting it off." Paying bills, having a hard conversation, going to the doctor — these are all things people commonly put off.

A famous saying you should know:

"Never put off till tomorrow what you can do today."

This is one of the most well-known English proverbs, and now you understand it perfectly.
Meaning 2: To Make Someone Lose Interest, Enthusiasm, or Appetite

This is the second most important meaning, and it is very different from the first. Here, "put off" means to repel, discourage, or disgust someone — to make them not want something anymore.

Think of it like pushing someone away from something emotionally.

Examples:

  • "The terrible smell put me off my food." (I lost my appetite because of it.)
  • "His rude behavior put her off immediately." (She lost interest in him.)
  • "The long waiting lines put me off visiting the museum."
  • "I was going to apply for the job, but the low salary put me off."

Notice that this meaning can work in two slightly different ways:

a) Someone is put off by something (a person, a thing, or a situation causes the feeling):

  • "I was put off by his arrogance."

b) Something puts you off doing something (you stop wanting to do a specific thing):

  • "The accident put me off driving for months."
  • "That bad experience put me off eating seafood."

Both are natural and very common.
Meaning 3: To Cause Someone to Dislike Something (Often Permanently)

This is closely related to Meaning 2, but the result is more lasting. Here, "put off" means something has caused you to develop a long-term dislike or aversion to something.

Examples:

  • "I had food poisoning from that restaurant, and it completely put me off spicy food."
  • "His dishonesty put her off relationships for a long time."
  • "One bad teacher can put a child off reading for years."

The key difference from Meaning 2 is the depth and duration. In Meaning 2, you just lose interest in a moment. In Meaning 3, the dislike tends to stick around.
Meaning 4: To Distract Someone and Break Their Concentration

Here, "put off" means to break someone's focus or disrupt their performance. You are "pushing away" their ability to concentrate.

Examples:

  • "Stop humming! You're putting me off." (You are distracting me.)
  • "The loud crowd put the tennis player off, and she made several mistakes."
  • "Don't put me off while I'm counting — I'll have to start again."

This meaning is very common in British English and appears often in sports contexts. It's about something external interrupting your mental focus.
Meaning 5: To Avoid Someone or Delay Dealing With Them (Using Excuses)

In this meaning, you "put someone off" by giving them excuses, delays, or vague promises instead of dealing with them directly. You are pushing the person away rather than dealing with the matter.

Examples:

  • "I've been trying to speak to the manager for a week, but they keep putting me off."
  • "She didn't want to say no, so she put him off by saying she was busy."
  • "Every time I asked for my money back, he put me off with excuses."

Notice that in this meaning, the object is always a person, not a thing.
Meaning 6: To Drop Someone Off a Vehicle (Uncommon but Real)

This is a less frequent meaning, but you may encounter it. It means to let someone get off a bus, train, or other vehicle — sometimes even against their will.

Examples:

  • "The conductor put the passenger off at the next stop because he had no ticket."
  • "The driver put us off at the wrong terminal."

You are unlikely to use this meaning in everyday conversation, but it's good to recognize it.
The Grammar of "Put Off" — Very Important

"Put off" is what's called a separable phrasal verb. This means the object (the thing or person you're talking about) can go in two positions:

Position A — Object after "off":

  • "I put off the meeting."
  • "She put off her appointment."

Position B — Object between "put" and "off":

  • "I put the meeting off."
  • "She put her appointment off."

Both are equally correct. However, there is one strict rule you must never break:

If the object is a pronoun (it, him, her, them, me, us), it MUST go in the middle. It can NEVER go after "off."

✅ "I put it off." (correct)
❌ "I put off it." (wrong — never say this)

✅ "His behavior put me off." (correct)
❌ "His behavior put off me." (wrong)

This rule applies to all separable phrasal verbs in English, so remembering it here will help you across the board.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

Since "put off" has multiple meanings, context is your best tool. Here are some quick clues:

  • If the object is a task, event, or plan → likely Meaning 1 (postpone).
  • If someone mentions feeling disgusted, repelled, or losing interest → Meaning 2 or 3.
  • If someone is talking about focus, concentration, or performance → Meaning 4.
  • If someone is being avoided or fobbed off with excuses → Meaning 5.
Common Collocations (Words Frequently Used Together With "Put Off")

Some things are very commonly "put off" in English. Knowing these combinations helps you sound natural:

  • Put off a meeting / appointment / trip / decision / task / payment / deadline / conversation / wedding
  • Put off doing homework / going to the doctor / making a call / starting a project
  • Be put off by someone's attitude / a smell / the price / bad reviews / a rude comment
Quick Summary of All Meanings

1. Postpone → "I put off the meeting."
2. Discourage / repel → "The price put me off buying it."
3. Cause lasting dislike → "That incident put me off flying forever."
4. Distract / break concentration → "Stop talking — you're putting me off."
5. Avoid someone with excuses → "They kept putting me off."
6. Drop off a vehicle → "The driver put them off at the station." (rare)
A Final Note on Tone

"Put off" in all its meanings carries a slightly negative or reluctant feeling. Postponing something usually implies you don't want to deal with it. Being put off means something has disappointed or repelled you. Being put off by someone means they failed to handle you properly. This underlying negativity is the emotional thread that runs through every meaning, and recognizing it will help you use "put off" with exactly the right nuance every time.
